title: Graph algorithms
text: Graph algorithms Four questions about the graph as a whole. FalkorDB computes the answers; the memory names what it finds and bounds the cost. Function Answers By -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------ groups(graph, kinds, relations=None, records=(), at_least=2, limit=100, show=100, at=None) Which things are linked, directly or through others: the sets, largest first algo.WCC important(graph, kinds, relation=None, limit=10, at=None) Which entities the most links point to, counting links from important ones more algo.pageRank between(graph, kinds, relations=None, limit=10, sample=None, seed=1, at=None) Which entities lie on the shortest paths between others algo.betweenness connection(graph, start, end, kinds=(), relations=None, max_hops=6, at=None) How two things are connected: the shortest chain, step by step shortestPath python from lighthouse import connection, groups, important groups(graph, [DEVICE], ["ABOUT"], records=["Episode"]) the episodes about the same devices important(graph, [DEVICE], "LOCATED_IN", limit=3) the rooms most devices were in connection(graph, (DEVICE, "d1"), (DEVICE, "d7")) through which rooms and teams A chain says what holds Without at , the four see every relation that was ever true. connection() says for each step whether the relation holds now, since when, and until when: python what connection() gives: one step for each relation of the chain [ "from": ("Device", "d1"), "relation": "LOCATED_IN", "to": ("Room", "r1"), "forward": True, "current": False, "since": ..., "until": ... ] At one time With at , each sees only the relations that held then and the entities that existed then. FalkorDB's algorithms cannot keep to the edges of one time, so the memory reads those relations in one query and runs the same algorithms itself. The tests check both against plain implementations. Fast the second time groups() , important() , and between() keep their answers until the graph grows where the question reads it. A graph only grows, so equal counts of nodes and edges mean the same graph; FalkorDB has those counts without a scan. On 100,000 entities and 550,000 relations on one laptop, the first answer took 77 ms for groups() , 64 ms for important() , and 233 ms for between() from 32 entities; the same question again took 0.2 to 0.3 ms. connection() took 0.5 ms for four steps. FalkorDB cannot stop these searches while they run, and writes wait for them. Do not let a model or a user choose their arguments without a limit on how often they ask.

title: Audit and time travel
text: Audit and time travel Every write keeps the version before it, and every entry names what it rests on. So the memory can answer questions about itself: what changed between two moments, what a change would do, what rested on a fact that turned out wrong, and how far an agent's work held. No model is asked; each answer is a few queries. Function Answers ---------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------ diff_between(graph, kinds, t1, t2) What was added, changed, linked, and unlinked between two moments what_if(graph, kinds, hypothetical_rows, at=None, situation=None) What rows would do to the graph's groups and ranking, without writing them impact_of_entry(graph, entry_id) Every entry, episode, handoff, lesson, and playbook that rests on an entry impact_of_state(graph, kind, key, since, until) The same for an entity, for what cited it during a stretch of time invalidate_entry(graph, entry_id, by, reason, at=None) Retracts an entry without deleting it, and gives its impact agent_trust(graph, agent) How far an agent's work held, from what the graph already records The examples go on from the earlier pages: device d1 was ok in room r1 , then hot in r2 , and episode d1-overheat records what the watcher, the forecaster, and the reviewer did about it. What changed between two moments python from lighthouse import diff_between day_one, day_two = "2026-01-01T12:00:00Z", "2026-01-02T12:00:00Z" diff_between(graph, [DEVICE], day_one, day_two)["values_changed"][0]["changed_keys"] ["status"] changes = diff_between(graph, [DEVICE], day_one, day_two) len(changes["relations_opened"]), len(changes["relations_closed"]) (1, 1): r2 opened, r1 closed The answer has entities_added , values_changed with the values before and after, relations_opened and relations_closed with their times, and the episodes opened and closed in between. It reads only the versions that began in the window, through the index on when a version begins. What a change would do what_if() lays rows over the graph as it is at at (now, by default) and compares: the groups that form (connected components), the entities whose importance (PageRank) shifts, and with situation , the playbooks that would fire. Nothing is written. python from lighthouse import what_if back = "key": "d1", "t": "2026-01-03T11:00:00Z", "values": "status": "hot", "note": "pump room sensor" , "relations": "LOCATED_IN": "r1" what_if(graph, [DEVICE], [(DEVICE, [back])], situation= "status": "hot" )["playbooks"][0]["name"] "hot-device" history(graph, DEVICE, "d1")[-1]["status"] "ok": nothing was written What rested on an entry The watcher's observation started the episode; the forecast cited it, and the reviewer's outcome cited the forecast. A lesson rests on the episode. python from lighthouse import impact_of_entry, impact_of_state impact_of_entry(graph, "d1-overheat/1")["downstream_entries"] ["d1-overheat/2", "d1-overheat/3"] impact_of_entry(graph, "d1-overheat/1")["lessons"][0]["at_risk"] True impact_of_state(graph, DEVICE, "d1", "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z", "2030-01-01T00:00:00Z")["direct_entries"] ["d1-overheat/1"] The search follows what was built on what: CITES from entry to evidence, FROM from a version to the entry it came from, POINTS_TO from a handoff, and SUPPORTED_BY from a lesson or a playbook. A handoff counts while it waits; one that was accepted is done. tainted_support counts the episodes in the impact that a lesson or playbook rests on. A lesson is at_risk when no episode it rests on is left outside the impact; a playbook, when fewer than three are, the evidence it needed to be written. Retract a fact, keep the record python from lighthouse import agent_trust, invalidate_entry retracted = invalidate_entry(graph, "d1-overheat/1", by="reviewer", reason="the sensor was miscalibrated") retracted: "id": "d1-overheat/1", "status": "invalidated", "impact": ... impact_of_entry(graph, "d1-overheat/1")["invalidated"] True episode(graph, "d1-overheat")["entries"][0]["invalidated_by"] "reviewer" invalidate_entry(graph, "d1-overheat/1", by="reviewer", reason="again")["status"] "exists" - Nothing is deleted. The entry gains invalidated_at , invalidated_by , and invalidated_why , and keeps everything else, so the record still says what the agent saw and why it acted. - A second retraction of the same entry is exists ; an entry that is not there is unknown , and the refusal is kept as a WriteFailure, like every refusal. - The memory marks only the entry. What to do with the records in its impact, such as reopening an episode or retiring a lesson, is your application's decision, made with the functions of the earlier pages. How far an agent's work held python agent_trust(graph, "watcher")["entries_invalidated"] 1 agent_trust(graph, "nobody")["score"] None: no evidence, nothing is known Four kinds of evidence are counted for and against an agent: entries it wrote against those later invalidated; closed episodes it wrote in that a lesson rests on, against those that contradict one; playbook runs it recorded that succeeded, against those that failed; and versions it wrote that held for at least a minute, against those replaced sooner. The score is the mean of the four rates, each smoothed as (for + 1) / (for + against + 2), over the kinds the agent has, so many versions do not drown a few failed runs. It reads only what the graph already holds; the name is not checked against anyone's identity. See [episodes and evidence](/episodes), [lessons and playbooks](/learning), and the [Python API](/reference impact_of_entry).

title: Benchmarks
text: Benchmarks Every number here comes from the running system, and every one can be run again. The measures live in the repository: cd backend && uv run python -m app.measure runs one against the FalkorDB of docker compose up -d (FalkorDB 6.0.2, pinned by digest) and writes its result, with the commit it ran on, to measurements/ .json . Each writes to throwaway graphs of its own. The results below are from one laptop, in a Linux container. Results Claim Measure Result --- --- --- Writing needs no model writes : 300 events of a live public feed, one at a time, counting model calls 0 model calls. One write: 5.2 ms at the median, 7.8 ms at the 95th percentile. 1,168 events a second in one batch. History is exact history : 500 entities and 7,711 changes, written in time order 7,711 facts read back, 0 wrong. Late rows are never placed wrong The same 7,711 changes, shuffled so that rows arrive late 3,167 late rows inserted in their place. 2,271 rows came after a later row had repeated the State they fall in; each was refused as stale and kept as a WriteFailure. 829 read-backs differ from the source, and every one of them involves a refused row: none is wrong without a record of why. Agents never double-claim claims : 16 agents, each on its own connection, race for 500 tasks 500 claims won, 0 tasks won twice. Tenants are isolated tenants : 200 rows in one tenant's graph, read from another's 0 nodes, 0 search results, 0 versions seen. Memory survives a restart restart , then docker compose restart falkordb , then restart --check The mark written before the restart is read after it, with FalkorDB's append-only file on. Graph-wide questions are fast 100,000 entities and 550,000 relations First answer: 77 ms for groups() , 64 ms for important() , 233 ms for between() from 32 entities. Asked again: 0.2 to 0.3 ms. connection() : 0.5 ms for four steps. A result that went against us memory replays 400 days of a public dataset of daily activity counts for many places through two agents built on the library: one watches the counts, one writes lessons from what ended. Each time a place turns unusually quiet or busy, each way of guessing says whether it is back to usual within 3 days, and the guess is scored when the spell ends. Guess Right 95% interval --- --- --- Always "it passes" (no memory) 5,141 of 5,258 (97.8%) 97.3 to 98.1% The lesson written about the place (memory) 5,141 of 5,258 (97.8%) 97.3 to 98.1% The place's own past spells (memory) 5,123 of 5,258 (97.4%) 97.0 to 97.8% Memory did not help on this task. A quiet or busy place almost always recovers within three days, so a guess with no memory is already near the ceiling; the lessons said the same as the base rate every time, and the place's own past did slightly worse. It is published as measured. Showing that memory helps needs a task where a place's past changes the answer. Comparing with other memory stacks There are no head-to-head numbers on this page yet, and none are borrowed from other projects' papers: a comparison is only fair on the same events, the same machine, and the same questions. What sets the designs apart can be measured directly: - Model calls per write. Memory layers that extract facts with a model, such as Mem0 and Graphiti by default, call a model on every write: latency in seconds and a cost per write. Lighthouse writes by rule, with no model: the writes measure above. - Exact answers about the past. Versions with a start and an end let as_of() give what was true at any moment; the history measure checks every fact against its source. - Coordination. Task claims and handoffs in one query each: the claims measure. Published benchmarks for agent memory, such as LoCoMo and LongMemEval, ask questions about long chat histories and score a model's answers. They test conversational recall with a model in the loop, which is a different job from keeping structured events by time, and Lighthouse has not been run on them. See [graph algorithms](/algorithms) for how the algorithm timings were taken, and [audit and time travel](/audit) for what the versions make possible.

title: Conversations
text: Conversations What was said, for each user, in order. The functions take the graph that holds the conversations: with one graph for each tenant, that is the graph of the tenant. python from lighthouse import say, messages, context, summarize, said, said_about say(graph, "ann", "main", "user", "why is d1 hot?", by="ann", mentions=[(DEVICE, "d1")]) say(graph, "ann", "main", "assistant", "the fan stopped", by="assistant", mentions=[(DEVICE, "d1")]) [m["text"] for m in messages(graph, "ann", "main")] ["why is d1 hot?", "the fan stopped"] said_about(graph, "ann", (DEVICE, "d1"))[0]["text"] "the fan stopped": newest first Function Does --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- say(graph, user, session_id, role, text, by, mentions=(), values=None, at=None) Adds one message. The first message opens the session. messages(graph, user, session_id, last=20, before=None) The last messages, oldest first. before reads further back. sessions(graph, user, limit=20) The sessions of the user, the one written to last first. said_about(graph, user, reference, limit=20) The messages that mention one thing, newest first. said(graph, user, question, limit=10, match="all") The messages whose text has the words of a question. summarize(graph, user, session_id, text, upto, by) Stores what the messages up to number upto come to. context(graph, user, session_id, last=20) What a model needs to go on: the summary, the messages after it, and how many wait to be summed up. forget_session(graph, user, session_id) Deletes one session and everything of it. forget_user(graph, user) Deletes everything the user said in the graph. What holds - A session belongs to one user, and every call names the user. Two users can both have a session main , and no id that one asks for reaches a session of the other. - A message takes its number and its place in one query: messages written at once by several writers get one order. - A mention is a name, not an edge: the thing may be in another graph. - The summary is your model's text; the memory holds no model. context() says with waiting when it is time to sum up again. A long session python def your_model_sums_up(texts): your model: the texts in, a short summary out return "ann asked why d1 was hot; the fan had stopped" kept = messages(graph, "ann", "main") summarize(graph, "ann", "main", your_model_sums_up([m["text"] for m in kept]), upto=kept[-1]["seq"], by="assistant") context(graph, "ann", "main")["summary"] "ann asked why d1 was hot; the fan had stopped" context() gives the summary, the messages after it, and with waiting how many older messages are not summed up yet: sum up again when it grows. [Models and agent integration](/integrations) has the whole loop. Forgetting Forgetting is the one place where the memory deletes what was written. forget_session() deletes the messages, the session and its summary, each reference that nothing else mentions, and what was kept of refused messages. After it, no property of any node or edge holds what the session held. Entities, episodes, and lessons are never deleted. Do not put there what a person may ask to have erased.

title: Tasks and handoffs
text: Tasks and handoffs Agents work together through the graph: a task is claimed by one agent, and a handoff passes a piece of the record to another. Tasks python from lighthouse import add_task, claim, complete, release add_task(graph, "check-d1", "check", ref="d1") add_task(graph, "report-d1", "report", ref="d1", after=["check-d1"]) waits for the first task = claim(graph, "agent-a", "check", lease=600) the oldest free task of the kind, or None complete(graph, "agent-a", task["id"]) only its owner can Function Does ----------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ add_task(graph, id, kind, ref=None, after=()) Adds an open task that waits for the tasks in after . False if the id exists. claim(graph, agent, kind, lease=None) Gives the oldest free task of a kind to an agent, for lease seconds or until done. complete(graph, agent, task_id) Marks a task done. Only its owner can, once. release(graph, agent, task_id) Gives a claimed task back. Only its owner can. - A task is claimed once. The claim is one query, and FalkorDB runs one write at a time on a graph: twelve agents racing for sixty tasks end with one owner each. - A task can only come after tasks that exist, so the order has no cycle. It is free once every task it comes after is done. - A claim with a lease holds that many seconds, at most seven days. After that another agent can claim it, and the first can no longer complete it. Handoffs A handoff points at what the receiver must read; it holds no copy. python from lighthouse import hand_off, handoffs_for, accept hand_off(graph, "h1", by="watcher", to="reviewer", points_to=[("Episode", "d1-overheat"), (DEVICE, "d1")], values= "ask": "Is d1 about to fail?" ) handoffs_for(graph, "reviewer") what waits for the reviewer, oldest first accept(graph, "h1", by="reviewer") "id": "h1", "status": "accepted" Status Meaning ---------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------- given The handoff was made exists A handoff with this id is there already, or its receiver accepted it before accepted The receiver took it refused An agent that is not the receiver tried to accept it unknown There is no such handoff missing Something it points at does not exist invalid It points at nothing, or its values cannot be stored - A handoff must point at something that exists: one that only carries text is refused. - accept() reads the receiver and marks the handoff in one query, so it is accepted once, by its receiver. - The names of agents are names your code gives. Set them from who is signed in, never from what a model wrote. See [security](/security).

title: Episodes and evidence
text: Episodes and evidence An episode is the record of one event: what agents saw, forecast, and did about it, in order, and how it ended. Each entry cites what it rested on, as it was at that moment. python from lighthouse import open_episode, record, close_episode, episode, episodes_about open_episode(graph, "d1-overheat", by="watcher", about=[(DEVICE, "d1")]) record(graph, "d1-overheat", "observation", by="watcher", values= "status": "hot" , cites=[(DEVICE, "d1")]) "id": "d1-overheat/1", "seq": 1, "status": "recorded" record(graph, "d1-overheat", "forecast", by="forecaster", values= "fails_in_hours": 6 , cites=["d1-overheat/1"]) close_episode(graph, "d1-overheat", by="reviewer", outcome= "failed": False , cites=["d1-overheat/2"]) episode(graph, "d1-overheat")["entries"] all three, in order, with what each cites episodes_about(graph, DEVICE, "d1")[0]["outcome"] "failed": False, ... Receipts Status Meaning ---------- --------------------------------------------------------- opened The episode was made exists An episode with this id is there already: nothing changed recorded The entry took the next number of the episode unknown The episode does not exist closed The episode has its outcome full The episode has 5,000 entries, the most one can hold missing Something in about or cites does not exist invalid The values, references, or time cannot be stored failed The database refused the query Every refusal is kept as a WriteFailure, with what was refused. What holds - An entry is appended with one query. Entries written at the same moment by several agents get one order, and no number is used twice. - Evidence must exist: an entry cannot cite a thing that is not in the graph. - A cited entity is pinned to the time of the entry. Reading it with as_of() at that time gives the version the agent saw, also after it changed. - An episode cannot be opened again after it is closed, and an entry cannot be changed. References Entries, episodes, and handoffs point at things with references, and episode() gives them back in the same form, so what is read can be cited. Reference Points at ------------------------------------------ ----------------------------------------------------- (Kind, key) An entity, pinned to the time of the entry or handoff "ep/3" or ("Entry", "ep/3") One entry ("Episode", "ep") A whole episode ("Lesson", id) , ("Playbook", "name 2") A lesson, or one version of a playbook Rows from what agents wrote extract(graph, kind, extractor, by, types=None, limit=100) reads entries it has not read yet and writes the rows that your function finds in them, by the write rule. Each State it adds points at its entry with FROM . The memory holds no model: the extractor is yours, a model or plain code.

title: FalkorDB behaviour
text: FalkorDB behaviour Lighthouse Memory builds its records and coordination rules on FalkorDB. The database supplies graph storage, traversal, indexes, and algorithms; the library supplies time-aware state, evidence records, write receipts, and agent memory semantics. Capabilities used by memory FalkorDB capability Lighthouse Memory use Guide ----------------------------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------- Property graph and Cypher traversal Follow entities, evidence, and versioned relationships [Memory model](/model) shortestPath , connected components, PageRank, betweenness Explain connections and inspect graph structure [Algorithms](/algorithms) Full-text indexes Recall entities, earlier states, entries, and messages by words [Recall](/recall) Vector indexes Retrieve semantic neighbours using your embedder [Semantic recall](/recall by-meaning) Independent graphs Separate tenant memory from shared context [Tenants](/tenants) Atomic single-query writes Allocate task claims and ordered record entries [Coordination](/coordination) Native algorithm results describe graph structure, not causal proof or business risk. Historical algorithm queries use the library's snapshot path because native algorithms cannot filter every relation by its validity window. Official references: [FalkorDB documentation](https://docs.falkordb.com/), [indexing](https://docs.falkordb.com/cypher/indexing), and [FalkorDB Python client](https://github.com/FalkorDB/falkordb-py). Tested behaviour The following observations were found by tests on the project's pinned image (graph module 60002, falkordb-py 1.7.1). They are version-specific observations, not claims about every FalkorDB release. The library works around them; revalidate when upgrading. Behaviour What the memory does -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ A node written while its index is being built is never added to that index: MATCH and MERGE by key miss it for good. Seen in 68 of 150 fresh graphs. ensure_schema() waits until every index is operational. Making an index or constraint while another is being made is refused: "another write is in progress". ensure_schema() asks again, until its deadline. Rows of one UNWIND do not see writes made for earlier rows of the same query. An entity is sent at most once per query. A pattern comprehension inside a FOREACH list corrupts the loop variable, with no error. Open edges are read with OPTIONAL MATCH and collect() before the writes. A pattern with an unnamed edge matches two nodes once, even with several parallel edges. Queries that count edges name the edge. localdatetime() rejects ...:11Z and keeps whole seconds; the client cannot send a datetime . Times are sent as text in UTC and converted in the query. A NUL byte in any parameter makes the server refuse the whole query. Text with a NUL is refused for its row only, before the query. A write cannot be stopped by a timeout, and it blocks every other writer of the graph. Each query carries a bounded load. The full-text index does not split words at a line break, a no-break space, or _ . The index reads the letters and digits of the text, one space between them. The full-text index reads a question as a query: matches everything. Only the letters and digits of a question are sent. A vector of another size than its index is stored without an error and never found. Vectors are checked against the kind's size first. The vector index searches with efRuntime 10 by default, and filters after the nearest k . The index is made with efRuntime 100; outdated vectors are taken out at the write. A timeout does not stop algo.WCC , algo.pageRank , or algo.betweenness . Each has a bounded cost, and answers are kept until the graph grows. An empty list of labels or edge types in an algorithm means all of them. No kind, or no relation, is an error before a query is built. An OPTIONAL MATCH right after an aggregating WITH finds nothing when it filters on a property of the node it matches. A plain WITH passes the aggregate on first. Aggregates beside a grouping key computed from the same variable all come back as the first aggregate. Keys are named in a WITH before the aggregates. algo.SPpaths took 240 to 2,500 ms for the fewest steps between two of 100,000 nodes. connection() uses shortestPath : 1 ms. UNWIND $ids AS i MATCH (x)-[o]-(y) WHERE id(x) = i traverses every edge: 970 ms where a seek takes 3 ms. Each node is found by its id first, then its edges. Inserting nodes under a unique constraint gets slower with every node of the label: 500 new nodes took about 40 ms in an empty label and about 575 ms with 5,500 there, against 2 ms with an index alone. The image tagged latest when this was measured did not slow down, but fails other tests of the library. Nothing yet: the constraint guards against a duplicate key, and the library keeps it. A batch of new entities costs more the more the kind holds; changes to entities that exist do not. A result longer than 10,000 rows is cut without a sign. Long reads are taken in pages.

title: Remember and read history
text: Remember and read history The write rule A row is the full picture of one entity at time t : "key", "t", "values", "relations", "entry" , with key and t required. What the row does not name is no longer true: a missing value is removed, a missing relation is closed. No model decides what a new fact replaces: a value replaces the same value of the same entity. remember(graph, kind, rows, by) returns one receipt per row, in order. Status Meaning Stored ----------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------- created First State of the entity Entity, State, relation edges changed The row differs from the current State and is later New State; the old one closed; changed relations closed or opened inserted The row came late: its time is inside an earlier State, or before the first A State in between, with relation edges cut or added for that stretch unchanged The content is already recorded for time t seen_last of the State, when t is later stale The row came late, after a later row that repeated the State it falls in WriteFailure conflict Another row with other content has the same time WriteFailure missing The entry the row names does not exist WriteFailure invalid The row cannot be stored WriteFailure failed The database refused the query WriteFailure What follows from the rule: - The same rows give the same history, however often they are sent. A replay is unchanged , not an error. So a feed can be read again and again, and only changes are written. - Rows that arrive in another order give the history of their times. The entity keeps the current values: a late row is never the current version. - A late row with a time before the State's seen_last is stale : the State held again after it, at a time the memory no longer knows exactly, so it is refused, never placed wrong. A source that sends only changes never repeats a State, and its late rows are always inserted . - A row can name the entry it comes from ( "entry": "look/3" ). The State it adds points at that entry with a FROM edge: the evidence of a fact. Reading Function Gives ---------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------- history(graph, kind, key) Every State of an entity, oldest first as_of(graph, kind, key, when) The State valid at when , or None related(graph, kind, key, relation, when=None) The keys the entity pointed at, now or at when pointing_at(graph, kind, relation, key, when=None) The keys of the entities that pointed at a target python from lighthouse import as_of, pointing_at, related as_of(graph, DEVICE, "d1", "2026-01-01T12:00:00Z")["status"] "ok" related(graph, DEVICE, "d1", "LOCATED_IN", "2026-01-01T12:00:00Z") ["r1"] pointing_at(graph, DEVICE, "LOCATED_IN", "r2") ["d1"] Partial updates update(graph, kind, key, t, by, values=None, relations=None, entry=None) changes what it names from t on and keeps the rest as the current State says. python from lighthouse import update d1 is hot in r2 since 2026-01-02 (the quickstart). Each update is later than that. update(graph, DEVICE, "d1", "2026-01-03T09:00:00Z", by="agent", values= "status": "ok" ) update(graph, DEVICE, "d1", "2026-01-03T10:00:00Z", by="agent", relations= "LOCATED_IN": "r3" ) as_of(graph, DEVICE, "d1", "2026-01-03T10:00:00Z")["note"] "pump room sensor": kept - A value of None is removed. A relation it names gets the targets it gives; a relation it does not name keeps its edges. - It reads the current State, makes the full row, and writes it by the rule. If another writer added a State in between, nothing is written and it reads again: a change is never written over one it did not see. After 5 tries it is busy , refused and stored. - It changes what is current: for an earlier time, send the full row to remember() . Times Send times as ISO text: 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z . The memory keeps whole seconds in UTC. A time more than five minutes ahead of the clock is refused: one row dated in the year 9999 would make every true row after it stale.

title: Models and agent integration
text: Models and agent integration Lighthouse Memory has no required language model and stores no provider API keys. Structured facts, history, episodes, and task coordination work without model calls. Your application owns the model client and passes the results or callbacks to the library. Three integration points Purpose Library contract Your responsibility ------------------------ ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Semantic recall embed() and nearest() receive a function mapping a list of texts to a list of vectors Choose an embedding model, keep its API key private, and declare the matching vector dimension Extract structured facts extract() receives your extractor function Validate model output against your schema and preserve source references Conversation summaries context() returns messages and a waiting count; summarize() stores your summary Choose the model and prompt, call it, and check the result before storage Keep the model boundary explicit python from lighthouse import context, messages, summarize def compact_session(graph, user, session_id, summarize_texts): held = context(graph, user, session_id, last=20) if not held["waiting"]: return older = messages( graph, user, session_id, last=held["waiting"], before=held["messages"][0]["seq"], ) text = summarize_texts(held["summary"], older) your model client summarize( graph, user, session_id, text, upto=held["upto"] + held["waiting"], by="summarizer", ) summarize_texts can call any provider or run locally. It must return a string. Resolve user and the tenant graph from authentication before calling this function. Embedding models Declare a Kind with text fields and the vector dimension returned by your embedder. Use one stable model identifier for indexing and retrieval. Changing model or dimension requires re-embedding; vectors from different models must not be mixed. See [semantic recall](/recall by-meaning) and the exact [embed API](/reference embed). Embedding calls happen off the structured write path. Tool-using agents Connect an MCP client to the hosted Memory service with a project key, or expose a small set of memory operations through your agent framework or [your own MCP server](/mcp). The model can choose a tool; trusted code executes it against an authorized graph and returns bounded evidence. Record observations, decisions, and outcomes in [episodes](/episodes). Keep model credentials on your server. Apply timeouts, spending limits, retries, and output validation in the client that owns the request. Lighthouse's write receipts describe storage outcomes; they do not certify a model's answer. Provider references These are model-client references, not dependencies or adapters shipped inside Lighthouse Memory: - [OpenAI API](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/): language models, function calling, and embeddings. - [Anthropic Claude API](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/overview): messages and tool use. - [Google Gemini API](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs): generation, function calling, and embeddings. - [Ollama](https://docs.ollama.com/): local and hosted model APIs. - [MCP specification and SDKs](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/getting-started/intro): typed tools for agent clients. Continue with [conversation memory](/conversations), [recall](/recall), or the [Python API](/reference).

title: Lessons and playbooks
text: Lessons and playbooks An episode is what happened. A lesson is what was learned from episodes. A playbook is what to do. The memory writes no lesson and no playbook of its own: an agent or a rule of your application says what was learned; the memory keeps the evidence, counts it, and ranks by it. Lessons python from lighthouse import learn, weigh, used, lessons_about learn(graph, "hot-in-r2", by="reviewer", statement="A hot device in room r2 did not fail.", supported_by=["d1-overheat"], about=[(DEVICE, "d1")]) lessons_about(graph, DEVICE, "d1")[0]["weight"] 1 Function Does ------------------------------------------------------------------ ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- learn(graph, id, by, statement, supported_by, about, values, at) Stores a lesson that rests on episodes that ended. At least one; a claim with no evidence is refused. weigh(graph, id, by, episode_id, agrees) One more episode for the lesson or against it. An episode counts once. used(graph, id, by, episode_id, helped=None) The lesson was used in an episode, and whether that helped. retire(graph, id, by, why) The lesson no longer holds. It stays, and is no longer given out. lesson(graph, id) The lesson with its weight and evidence. lessons_about(graph, kind, key, at_least=1, since=None) The lessons about an entity that still hold, heaviest first. The weight is the episodes that agree, minus those that do not, plus the uses that helped, minus those that did not. A lesson below at_least is no longer given out. With since , lessons that nothing touched since then fade. Playbooks Writing what an agent will do is riskier than writing what it knows. A playbook has four guards. Guard How ----------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Enough evidence write_playbook() needs 3 episodes that ended ( needs changes it, never below 1). Never changed A write makes the next version and switches the one before off. An off switch switch(graph, name, by, on=False) . A stop of its own After 3 failures in a row it switches itself off, in the query that records the failure. python from lighthouse import close_episode, open_episode, playbooks_for, ran, write_playbook A playbook rests on episodes that ended: three of them, unless needs says otherwise. for name in ("e1", "e2", "e3"): open_episode(graph, name, by="watcher", about=[(DEVICE, "d1")]) close_episode(graph, name, by="reviewer", outcome= "cause": "fan", "fixed": True ) write_playbook(graph, "hot-device", by="reviewer", trigger= "status": "hot" , steps=[ "do": "check the fan" ], supported_by=["e1", "e2", "e3"]) playbooks_for(graph, "status": "hot", "room": "r2" )[0]["steps"] [ "do": "check the fan" ] open_episode(graph, "e4", by="watcher", about=[(DEVICE, "d1")]) ran(graph, "hot-device", by="watcher", episode_id="e4", succeeded=True) A trigger fits a situation when every property of the trigger is in the situation with the same value. Promotion What repeats in episodes that ended becomes a lesson or a playbook. The memory cannot tell what a repeat is, so you pass a rule: a function of one ended episode that says what it shows. python from lighthouse import promote def rule(episode): outcome = episode["entries"][-1] if "cause" not in outcome: this episode says nothing about a cause return [] return [ "lesson": "d1-fan", "statement": "d1 gets hot because of its fan", "about": [(DEVICE, "d1")], "agrees": outcome["cause"] == "fan" , "playbook": "cool-d1", "trigger": "status": "hot", "device": "d1" , "steps": [ "do": "clean the fan" ] , ] promote(graph, "reviewer", rule, at_least=3) e1, e2, e3 agree: the lesson and the playbook - A lesson is learned when at_least episodes agree with it; after that each episode weighs it. - A playbook is written when at_least episodes show the same trigger and steps. - For a playbook that ran in the episode, a rule can also return "ran": name, "succeeded": bool : that judges the run. - Every episode counts once, so promote() can run after every read of a source and writes nothing twice.

title: Quickstart
text: Quickstart The memory is the Python package lighthouse , published on PyPI as lighthouse-graph . It depends on one package, the FalkorDB client, and needs Python 3.12 or later and a running FalkorDB. Using project API keys instead? See the [Memory HTTP API](/memory-api). This quickstart covers direct Python access. Install bash pip install lighthouse-graph or with uv: bash uv add lighthouse-graph The package is installed as lighthouse-graph and imported as lighthouse . To change the library itself, install it from a clone of the repository instead: pip install -e lighthouse-memory . Start FalkorDB The memory keeps everything in FalkorDB. For a local one, with Docker: bash docker run -p 6379:6379 -p 3000:3000 -it --rm falkordb/falkordb:6.0.2 It listens on port 6379 , with FalkorDB Browser on http://localhost:3000 . The library is tested on FalkorDB 6.0.2; newer images behave differently in ways the [FalkorDB page](/falkordb) lists, so keep to this one until the library says otherwise. --rm throws its data away when it stops: for data that must stay, see the [official installation guide](https://docs.falkordb.com/), or use a managed instance. The examples below connect to 127.0.0.1:6379 ; use your own host, port, and credentials. Declare what you remember A Kind is a kind of thing: its label, the property that identifies one, the values that are times, the relations it has to other kinds, and the values that can be searched by their words. python from falkordb import FalkorDB from lighthouse import Kind, ensure_schema, remember, history, as_of, related ROOM = Kind("Room", key="code") DEVICE = Kind( "Device", key="serial", times=("last_seen",), text=("note",), relations= "LOCATED_IN": ROOM , ) graph = FalkorDB(host="127.0.0.1", port=6379).select_graph("world") ensure_schema(graph, [DEVICE]) once, before the first write ensure_schema() makes the unique key of each kind and the indexes the memory reads, and returns only when they are ready. Call it on every start; it changes nothing that is there. Write rows A row is the whole picture of one thing at one time. Send rows as they come; the memory works out what changed. python remember(graph, DEVICE, by="inventory", rows=[ "key": "d1", "t": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z", "values": "status": "ok", "note": "pump room sensor" , "relations": "LOCATED_IN": "r1" , ]) [ "key": "d1", "status": "created" ] remember(graph, DEVICE, by="inventory", rows=[ "key": "d1", "t": "2026-01-02T00:00:00Z", "values": "status": "hot", "note": "pump room sensor" , "relations": "LOCATED_IN": "r2" , ]) [ "key": "d1", "status": "changed" ] Each row gets a receipt. A row that cannot be stored is never lost silently: it is kept as a WriteFailure in the graph, with the reason. Read it back, at any time python history(graph, DEVICE, "d1") both versions, oldest first as_of(graph, DEVICE, "d1", "2026-01-01T12:00:00Z")["status"] "ok" related(graph, DEVICE, "d1", "LOCATED_IN") ["r2"] related(graph, DEVICE, "d1", "LOCATED_IN", "2026-01-01T12:00:00Z") ["r1"] Next - [The memory model](/model): what is in the graph. - [Remember and read history](/history): the write rule, late rows, and partial updates. - [Episodes and evidence](/episodes): what agents saw and did.

title: Agents, MCP, and plugins
text: Agents, MCP, and plugins Agents reach Lighthouse Memory in two ways. The hosted Memory service has an MCP endpoint: any MCP client connects to a project with that project's API key, and no code is needed. Or you serve the library's functions from your own MCP server, next to your own graph. The hosted MCP endpoint The Memory service answers MCP over streamable HTTP at /mcp , beside its HTTP API: https:// /mcp , or http://localhost:8200/mcp for a local one. The console shows the address of yours under Agents & MCP . - The key is the agent. Send a project API key as a bearer token. The key chooses the project, its scopes choose what the tools may do, and its name is the agent's name in every entry, claim, and handoff. Create one key per agent and name it after the agent. A tool cannot write under another name. - The same rules as the HTTP API. Each MCP request counts against the key's 120 requests a minute and shows in the project's usage. Refusals give the same short messages as the HTTP API; details stay in the service's logs. - What tools return is data. Memories and entries were written by people and other agents. The server tells the model to treat them as data, never as instructions. Tool Access Does ----------------------------------------------------------- ------ -------------------------------------------------------- remember(key, title, text, metadata, links) write Saves a memory, or a new version of one recall(query) read Memories whose title or text has the words, up to 100 history(key) read Every version of a memory, oldest first connection(start, end) read The shortest chain of links between two memories open_episode(id, about) write Starts an episode about memories that exist record(episode_id, type, values, cites) write Adds an entry that cites its evidence close_episode(episode_id, outcome, cites) write Closes an episode with its outcome episode(episode_id) , episodes_about(key) read One episode with its entries; the episodes about a memory add_task(id, kind, about, after) , claim_task(kind, lease) write Adds work; claims the oldest free task of a kind complete_task(task_id) , release_task(task_id) write Finishes or gives back a task the agent holds hand_off(id, to, points_to, values) , accept_handoff(id) write Passes work to another agent; takes work given to it handoffs(waiting) read The handoffs given to this agent A key with read access only can call the read tools; a write tool answers that the key does not allow it. Connect a client Replace the address and YOUR_PROJECT_API_KEY with yours. The console fills both in when you create a key for an agent on its Agents & MCP page. Claude Code , in a terminal: bash claude mcp add --transport http lighthouse-memory https://memory.example.com/mcp \ --header "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_PROJECT_API_KEY" Cursor ( ~/.cursor/mcp.json or .cursor/mcp.json ): json "mcpServers": "lighthouse-memory": "url": "https://memory.example.com/mcp", "headers": "Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_PROJECT_API_KEY" Codex ( ~/.codex/config.toml ) reads the key from the environment variable it names: toml [mcp_servers.lighthouse-memory] url = "https://memory.example.com/mcp" bearer_token_env_var = "LIGHTHOUSE_API_KEY" Claude Desktop connects to a server that needs a header through mcp-remote , which needs Node.js. In claude_desktop_config.json : json "mcpServers": "lighthouse-memory": "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "mcp-remote", "https://memory.example.com/mcp", "--header", "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_PROJECT_API_KEY"] Your own agent , with the MCP SDK for Python: bash pip install "mcp>=1.26, =1.26, str: """Read a device now or at a UTC timestamp.""" return json.dumps(as_of(graph, DEVICE, serial, at or now()), default=str) @server.tool() def device_history(serial: str) -> str: """Read the recorded state changes of a device.""" return json.dumps(history(graph, DEVICE, serial), default=str) if __name__ == "__main__": server.run(transport="stdio") Agent needs Library functions ---------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------- Resolve an entity from text search() , search_history() Inspect state and changes as_of() , history() , related() Follow shared evidence pointing_at() , similar() , connection() Inspect a group or structural importance groups() , important() Read prior outcomes episode() , lessons_about() , playbooks_for() Check what rested on a fact impact_of_entry() , diff_between() Append a decision or hand off work record() , add_task() , hand_off() Choose the graph from an authenticated identity before a tool runs, and set the agent's name in server code. Do not accept raw queries, graph names, credentials, or agent names from a model's arguments. Bound the results and the number of calls, catch infrastructure errors in the wrapper, and give the agent a short explanation; keep diagnostics in your logs. See [model integration](/integrations), [audit and time travel](/audit), [security](/security), and the [official MCP Python SDK](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk).

title: Memory HTTP API
text: Memory HTTP API The Lighthouse Memory service exposes project-scoped structured memories over HTTP. Its developer console is a separate website from this documentation. The Python library connects directly to FalkorDB; it does not require a Lighthouse API key. Create a project key Open the Memory console, create a project, then choose API keys → Create API key . Name the key, select read and/or write access, and choose its expiry. Copy the secret once and keep it in your application server’s environment. The console lists only a prefix after creation. Revoke unused keys from the same page. A key selects exactly one project graph. Clients cannot change the project using a request parameter. Account sessions and project keys are different credentials: sessions access your console; keys access the /v1 memory endpoints. Store a memory Use your service address as LIGHTHOUSE_MEMORY_URL and your key as LIGHTHOUSE_MEMORY_KEY . This example is a request format; no request is sent by this page. bash curl "$LIGHTHOUSE_MEMORY_URL/v1/memories" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $LIGHTHOUSE_MEMORY_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d ' "key":"decision-001","title":"Preferred language","text":"Use Python examples.","metadata": "source":"user preference" ,"links":[] ' Reusing an identifier writes a new version when its values change. Writes use UTC whole-second observation times. Conflicting updates to one identifier within the same second are refused; retry after the clock advances. Earlier versions remain available through history. links contains identifiers already stored in the same project and replaces that memory’s current outgoing connections. Read and follow connections Method Endpoint Scope Result ------ ------------------------------------------------- -------------- ------------------------------------------------------- POST /v1/memories memory:write Write receipt: created, changed, unchanged, or inserted GET /v1/memories?q=python memory:read Up to 100 memories; optional full-text search GET /v1/memories/decision-001/history memory:read Stored versions in data GET /v1/connections?start=note-002&end=decision-001 memory:read Connection paths, bounded to six hops, in data List responses include data and limit . No pagination is currently available. The console’s usage page records successful memory operations; it is an activity record, not a billing meter. Failed and refused requests are not included in those totals. Coordinate agents A project key also acts as one agent, named by the key: create one key per agent, such as watcher or reviewer . The key decides who wrote an entry, who holds a task, and who gives or accepts a handoff. A request cannot name another writer. An episode records one event in order. Start it about memories that exist, append entries that cite their evidence, and close it with an outcome: bash curl "$LIGHTHOUSE_MEMORY_URL/v1/episodes/overload-1/entries" -H "Authorization: Bearer $LIGHTHOUSE_MEMORY_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d ' "type":"observation","values": "expected":5 ,"cites": "memories":["pump-2"],"entries":[],"episodes":[] ' Method Endpoint Scope Result ------ -------------------------------------- -------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------- POST /v1/episodes memory:write "id","about":[memory ids] starts an episode: opened or exists POST /v1/episodes/overload-1/entries memory:write Appends an entry; the receipt names it overload-1/1 , overload-1/2 … POST /v1/episodes/overload-1/close memory:write Records "outcome": … as the last entry; the episode takes no more GET /v1/episodes/overload-1 memory:read The episode with its entries in order, each with what it cites GET /v1/memories/pump-2/episodes memory:read Episodes about one memory, newest first, each with its outcome POST /v1/tasks memory:write "id","kind","about","after":[task ids] adds an open task POST /v1/tasks/claim memory:write "kind","lease" gives this agent the oldest free task, or null POST /v1/tasks/review-1/complete memory:write Marks the task done; only the agent that holds it can POST /v1/tasks/review-1/release memory:write Opens the task again for another agent POST /v1/handoffs memory:write "id","to","points_to": … ,"values": … passes work to an agent GET /v1/handoffs?waiting=true memory:read Handoffs given to this agent, oldest first; false includes accepted POST /v1/handoffs/h1/accept memory:write Accepts a handoff given to this agent, once cites and points_to name entry ids, episode ids, and memory ids, each of which must exist in the project. A claim is one atomic step, so two agents never hold the same task. A task with after waits until those tasks are done. A claim with a lease in seconds, up to seven days, can be taken by another agent once it runs out. Limits and errors Requests are bounded to 64 KiB. Identifiers contain 1–100 characters: letters, digits, _ , . , : , / , or - , starting with a letter or digit. Titles support 200 characters, memory text 12,000 characters, metadata 12,000 JSON characters, and each memory up to 50 outgoing connections. Episode, task, and handoff ids follow the same rule without / , because an entry id is the episode id, / , and its number. Each project key permits 120 authenticated requests per UTC minute. Invalid credentials return 401 ; insufficient scope, or a handoff given to another agent, returns 403 ; an unknown episode or handoff returns 404 ; a closed episode, or a task this agent does not hold, returns 409 ; invalid input or a reference that does not exist returns 422 ; excessive request size returns 413 ; request limits return 429 . Service failures return a safe 503 message, with diagnostic details kept in server logs. The same operations are MCP tools at /mcp , for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Claude Desktop, and your own agents: see [agents, MCP, and plugins](/mcp). The HTTP service covers structured writes, text search, history, connection paths, episodes, tasks, and handoffs. Lessons, playbooks, promotion, conversations, and semantic recall are available through the [Python library](/reference), not these HTTP endpoints. Preview status The current service is a developer preview, free while billing is not active. Managed hosting plans, email verification, password recovery, and team invitations are not active yet. An account has up to 5 workspaces, each with up to 20 projects; each project has a separate graph and up to 20 active keys, with expiry between 1 and 365 days. A project or a workspace can be deleted from the console's settings, after typing its name. Deleting a project deletes its graph, with every memory and version, its keys, and its usage; deleting a workspace deletes its projects. An account's only workspace cannot be deleted. See [security and limits](/security), [tenant graphs](/tenants), and [the library quickstart](/library) for direct FalkorDB integration.

title: The memory model
text: The memory model Everything the memory holds is nodes and edges of one FalkorDB graph. Knowing them lets you read the graph in the FalkorDB browser, and write your own queries where the API has none. Things and their versions - An entity is a node with the label and key of its Kind , and the label Entity that all entities share. It holds the current values, so a query or an index on the entity sees what is true now. - A State is one version of the entity's values. It has valid_from , and valid_to once a later version replaced it. The States of one entity form a chain through NEXT , and the entity points at each with HAS_STATE . seen_last is the last time a row repeated the State. - A relation is an edge from one entity to another with its own valid_from and valid_to . A relation that did not change keeps its edge when another value changes. - by on every State and relation edge names who wrote it. recorded_at is when the memory stored it; valid_from is when the fact became true. text (Device d1) -HAS_STATE-> (State, valid_from 1 Jan, valid_to 2 Jan) -NEXT-> (State, valid_from 2 Jan) (Device d1) -LOCATED_IN valid_from 1 Jan, valid_to 2 Jan -> (Room r1) (Device d1) -LOCATED_IN valid_from 2 Jan -> (Room r2) What agents saw and did - An episode is the record of one event, ABOUT the entities it concerns. Its entries are numbered in the order they were written, through HAS and NEXT : an observation, a forecast, an action, or any type the application names. The entry of type outcome closes the episode. - An entry cites its evidence with CITES edges: earlier entries, other episodes, lessons, and entities. A cited entity is pinned to the time of the entry, so as_of() gives the version the agent saw. The Agent that wrote an entry has a WROTE edge to it. - A lesson is what was learned from episodes that ended. It points at the episodes for it and against it, and at the episodes where it was used. - A playbook is what to do when a situation comes again: a trigger, ordered steps, and the episodes it was drawn from. A new version replaces the one before; no version is ever changed. How agents work together - A task is work that one agent claims. It can wait for other tasks ( AFTER ), and every claim stays as a CLAIMED_BY edge. - A handoff passes work from one agent ( GAVE ) to another ( TO ). It points at entries, episodes, and entities with POINTS_TO , and holds no copy of them. What people said - A session holds what was said with one user, as messages in order, and one summary of the messages up to a number. - A message mentions things by name: a Reference holds the label and key of a thing, and no edge to it, because the thing may be in another graph. Bookkeeping - A WriteFailure is a write that did not happen: the reason, the kind, the key, and up to 2,000 characters of what was refused. The same refusal again is counted on the same node ( times , last_at ). - A Stamp is one node with a random id that ensure_schema() gives a graph once. A graph that is deleted and made again under its name has another stamp. - Times are FalkorDB localdatetime values in UTC, in whole seconds. Graphs One FalkorDB holds many graphs. The application chooses which: by default one graph, world , that everyone may read, and one graph for each tenant. See [tenants](/tenants).

title: Recall
text: Recall Four ways to find what is in memory: by the graph, by words, by meaning, and one ranking from all three. Function Finds -------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- pointing_at(graph, kind, relation, key, when=None) The entities whose relation pointed at a target, now or at when similar(graph, kind, key, relations=None, limit=10) Entities of the same kind that share relation targets with one, most shared first, with what they share search(graph, kind, question, limit=10, match="all") Entities whose text has the words of a question search_history(graph, kind, question, limit=10, match="all") Versions whose text had the words, now or earlier, with when each held search_entries(graph, question, limit=10, match="all") Entries of episodes whose text has the words nearest(graph, kind, question, embedder, model, limit=10) Entities whose text is closest in meaning, with the similarity nearest_entries(graph, question, embedder, model, limit=10) Entries whose text is closest in meaning fuse(rankings, limit=10) One ranking from several, by the place each gave By words search() reads FalkorDB's full-text index over the values a Kind names in text . A question is never sent to the index as it is: only its letters and digits, at most 20 words. So does not list everything, and a question cannot choose a field. match="any" finds what has one of the words. A renamed thing is found by its new name with search() , and by its old one with search_history() , which says when each name held. By meaning The memory holds no model: you pass a function that turns texts into vectors. python from lighthouse import Kind, embed, ensure_schema, nearest, remember dimensions is the size of your model's vectors: 384, 768, or more. 3 for this stand-in. MANUAL = Kind("Manual", key="code", text=("title", "body"), dimensions=3) ensure_schema(graph, [MANUAL]) remember(graph, MANUAL, by="docs", rows=[ "key": "m1", "t": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z", "values": "title": "Pump seals", "body": "Replace a seal that leaks." , "key": "m2", "t": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z", "values": "title": "Fan care", "body": "Clean the fan every month." , ]) def embedder(texts): your model: texts in, one vector for each out. A stand-in here. return [[t.count("s") + 1.0, t.count("e") + 1.0, t.count("a") + 1.0] for t in texts] embed(graph, MANUAL, embedder, model="stand-in") off the write path: remember() never asks a model nearest(graph, MANUAL, "the seal of my pump leaks", embedder, model="stand-in")[0]["key"] - embed() gives a vector to each entity whose text has none. remember() never asks a model. - A write that changes the text takes its vector out of the index in the same query, so nearest() never answers from text that is gone. - Vectors of another model are never compared. All three python from lighthouse import fuse, search, similar fuse( "graph": similar(graph, DEVICE, "d1"), devices that share d1's rooms and teams "words": search(graph, DEVICE, "pump sensor"), devices whose note has the words ) add "meaning": nearest(...) for a kind with dimensions The scores of the three cannot be compared, so fuse() uses only the places (reciprocal rank fusion), and says which ranking put each result where.

title: Python API
text:
Kind(label: str, key: str = 'key', times: tuple[str, ...] = (), relations: dict = <factory>, text: tuple[str, ...] = (), dimensions: int = 0) -> None A kind of entity, declared once by the application.

label      node label
key        property that identifies one entity
times      values that are stored as native time values
relations  {TYPE: Kind}: edges from this kind to another, each with a validity window.
           Use SELF for a relation to the same kind: `{"KNOWS": SELF}`
text       values that can be searched by their words
dimensions size of the vectors that stand for that text; 0 for no search by meaning

A Kind cannot change after it is made: its names were checked once and go into queries. SELF = 'self' WORLD = 'world' ensure_schema(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, kinds=(), wait_seconds: float = 10.0, entry_dimensions: int = 0) -> None Create a unique constraint on the key of every kind, a full-text index on the text
of every kind and of its States, a vector index for every kind with dimensions, and the
engine's own indexes, among them the full-text index of entries. With `entry_dimensions`,
entries get a vector index of that size too, for embed_entries() and nearest_entries(). Give the graph its stamp, once.
A duplicate key then fails the whole query. Safe to call on every start.

Call it before the first write. When it adds a kind to a graph that is in use, stop
the writers first: a write during the build of an index is lost from that index. tenant(db: falkordb.falkordb.FalkorDB, tenant_id: str) -> falkordb.graph.Graph The private graph of one tenant. FalkorDB accepts any graph name, so the identifier
is checked here: a tenant can never name the world graph or another tenant's graph. world(db: falkordb.falkordb.FalkorDB) -> falkordb.graph.Graph The graph every tenant may read. record_failure(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, reason: str, kind: str | None = None, key=None, detail=None, owner=None) Store a write that did not happen, so it is never lost silently.

What is stored is bounded and safe, whatever the refused write held: `detail` is cut to
2,000 characters, and a kind or key that is not a valid one is left out. `owner` names
the user whose content the refused write held, so that it can be erased with the rest. remember(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, kind: lighthouse.kinds.Kind, rows, by: str) -> list[dict] Store what is true about entities of one kind, from the time `t` of each row.

A row is {"key", "t", "values", "relations", "entry"}; key and t are required.
  values     properties of the entity. Null or missing means the value is absent.
  relations  {TYPE: key or list of keys} of the entities it points at, for the types
             declared in the Kind. Missing means it points at none.
  entry      the id of the entry the row comes from, such as an observation. A State
             that the row adds points at that entry, as its evidence.
A row is the full picture at time t: what it does not name is no longer true.
`by` names the agent or source that writes. It is stored on every State and edge.

Returns one receipt per row, in order: {"key", "status"} with status
  created    first State of the entity
  changed    the row differs: the current State is closed and a new one added
  inserted   the row came late: it is put into the history at its time
  unchanged  the row is already recorded for that time
  stale      the row came late, after a row with a later time that repeated what held
             before it: where it ends is not known, so it is refused
  conflict   another row with other content has the same time: refused
  missing    the entry it names does not exist: refused
  invalid    the row cannot be stored
  failed     the database refused the query
Stale, conflicting, missing, invalid, and failed rows leave a WriteFailure node. update(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, kind: lighthouse.kinds.Kind, key, t, by: str, values=None, relations=None, entry=None) -> dict Change the values and relations it names, from time `t` on. A value of None removes
it. A relation that it names gets the targets it gives, and keeps none other. The rest
stays as the current State says. An entity that does not exist starts with what the
update names.

Returns a receipt as remember() does. Besides, it can say
  stale  `t` is before the current State: an update changes what is current. Send the
         full row of that time to remember() instead.
  busy   other writers changed the entity each time it was read: refused as_of(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, kind: lighthouse.kinds.Kind, key, when) -> dict | None The State that was valid at `when`, or None if the entity was not known then. history(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, kind: lighthouse.kinds.Kind, key) -> list[dict] Every State of an entity, oldest first. A State that a row with an entry added has
"entry": the id of that entry. related(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, kind: lighthouse.kinds.Kind, key, relation: str, when=None) -> list Keys of the entities that `key` pointed at through `relation` at `when` (default: now). embed(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, kind: lighthouse.kinds.Kind, embedder, model: str, limit: int = 100) -> dict Give a vector to entities of `kind` whose text has none, or whose text or model has
changed since. At most `limit` in one call. Returns {"embedded", "waiting"}: how many
got a vector now, and how many still wait. Run it off the write path until none wait.

`embedder` takes a list of texts and returns one vector for each, of kind.dimensions
numbers. `model` names what made them. A call with another model than the last one
reads the kind once, to give every entity with text a vector of the new model. embed_entries(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, embedder, model: str, limit: int = 100) -> dict Give a vector to entries whose text has none of this model, at most `limit` in one
call, in the order they were stored. Returns {"embedded", "waiting"}, as embed() does.
Run it off the write path until none wait.

It reads the entries stored since its mark for this model: a model it has not seen
starts from the first entry. fuse(rankings: dict[str, list[dict]], limit: int = 10) -> list[dict] Merge rankings of the same kind of entity, best first:
[{"key", "score", "places"}]. `rankings` maps a name to the result of similar(),
search(), or nearest(). "places" maps each ranking's name to the place it gave the
entity, from 1. nearest(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, kind: lighthouse.kinds.Kind, question: str, embedder, model: str, limit: int = 10) -> list[dict] Entities of `kind` whose text is closest in meaning to `question`, closest first:
[{"key", "score", "values"}]. The score is the cosine similarity: 1 for the same
direction, 0 for none in common.

An entity whose text changed after its vector was made is left out until embed() runs
again. So is a vector of another model. A question without text finds nothing.
At most 1,000 vectors are read: after a change of model, run embed() to the end first. nearest_entries(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, question: str, embedder, model: str, limit: int = 10) -> list Entries whose text is closest in meaning to `question`, closest first:
[{"id", "score", "entry"}], with the score as nearest() gives it. Vectors of another
model are left out, and at most 1,000 vectors are read. pointing_at(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, kind: lighthouse.kinds.Kind, relation: str, key, when=None) -> list Keys of the entities of `kind` whose `relation` pointed at `key` at `when` (default:
now). The reverse of related(): related() asks where one entity points, this asks what
points at one target. search(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, kind: lighthouse.kinds.Kind, question: str, limit: int = 10, match: str = 'all') -> list[dict] Entities of `kind` whose text has the words of `question`, best first:
[{"key", "score", "values"}]. "values" holds the current values of the entity.

  match  "all": every word must be there. "any": one word is enough.

Words are matched whole and in their base form: "sensors" finds "sensor". A question
without a letter or digit finds nothing. search_entries(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, question: str, limit: int = 10, match: str = 'all') -> list[dict] Entries of episodes whose values had the words of `question`, best first:
[{"id", "score", "entry"}]. "entry" holds the properties of the entry, as episode()
gives them, without its evidence. search_history(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, kind: lighthouse.kinds.Kind, question: str, limit: int = 10, match: str = 'all') -> list[dict] States of entities of `kind` whose text had the words of `question`, the current one
or an earlier one, best first: [{"key", "score", "state"}]. "state" is the State as
history() gives it, with its validity window.

Words are matched as search() matches them. similar(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, kind: lighthouse.kinds.Kind, key, relations=None, limit: int = 10) -> list[dict] Entities of the same kind that share relation targets with this one, most shared
first: [{"key", "shared", "through"}]. "through" lists what is shared, as
(relation, key of the target), so the reason can be shown.

This entity's current relations are compared with every relation the others ever had,
so entities of the past are found. `relations` narrows the relations that count. close_episode(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, episode_id: str, by: str, outcome=None, cites=(), at=None) -> dict Record what the event ended in, and close the episode. The outcome is the last entry.
Returns the same receipt as record(). episode(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, episode_id: str) -> dict | None An episode with its entries in order, or None if it does not exist. Each entry has
"cites": the (label, key) pairs it rests on. "about" has the same form. episodes_about(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, kind: lighthouse.kinds.Kind, key) -> list[dict] The episodes about one entity, newest first. Each has "outcome": the entry that
closed it, or None while it is open. open_episode(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, episode_id: str, by: str, about=(), at=None) -> dict Start the record of one event. `about` lists the entities it concerns, as (Kind, key).

Returns a receipt {"id", "status"} with status
  opened   the episode was made
  exists   an episode with this id is there already; nothing changed
  missing  an entity in `about` does not exist: refused
  invalid  `about` or `at` cannot be used: refused
  failed   the database refused the query
Missing, invalid, and failed leave a WriteFailure node. record(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, episode_id: str, entry_type: str, by: str, values=None, cites=(), at=None) -> dict Append one entry to an episode: an observation, a forecast, an action, or any other
type the application names.

  values  properties of the entry
  cites   the evidence: ids of earlier entries, entities as (Kind, key), and other
          episodes as ("Episode", id)
  at      when it happened (default: now)

Returns a receipt. {"id", "seq", "status": "recorded"} when stored. Otherwise
{"id": None, "status", "reason"} with status
  unknown  the episode does not exist
  closed   the episode is closed
  full     the episode has 5,000 entries
  missing  something in `cites` does not exist
  invalid  `values`, `cites`, or `at` cannot be stored
  failed   the database refused the query
and a WriteFailure node that holds the refused entry. extract(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, kind: lighthouse.kinds.Kind, extractor, by: str, types=None, limit: int = 100) -> dict Read entries with text that were not read for `kind` yet, in the order they were
stored, at most `limit` of them, and write the rows that `extractor` finds in each.

  extractor  a function of one entry (its properties: id, type, at, by, and its values)
             that returns a list of rows of `kind`, as remember() takes them. A row
             without "t" is true from the time of the entry. Its "entry" is the entry.
  types      the types of entries to read, such as ["observation"] (default: all)

Returns {"read", "rows", "waiting"}: how many entries were read, how many rows came back
with each status of remember(), and how many entries still wait. An extractor that
raises stops the call; the entry it read stays waiting, and the ones before it are done. accept(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, handoff_id: str, by: str) -> dict Take a handoff. Returns a receipt {"id", "status"} with status
  accepted  the handoff is now accepted by the agent it was given to
  exists    that agent accepted it before; nothing changed
  refused   it was given to another agent
  unknown   there is no such handoff
Refused and unknown leave a WriteFailure node that names who tried. hand_off(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, handoff_id: str, by: str, to: str, points_to, values=None, at=None) -> dict Pass work from agent `by` to agent `to`.

  points_to  what the receiver must read: entry ids, ("Episode", id), and entities as
             (Kind, key). At least one. An entity is pinned to the time of the handoff.
  values     short properties of the handoff, such as what is asked
  at         when it was given (default: now)

Returns a receipt {"id", "status"} with status
  given    the handoff was made
  exists   a handoff with this id is there already; nothing changed
  missing  something in `points_to` does not exist: refused
  invalid  it points at nothing, or the values, references, or time cannot be stored
  failed   the database refused the query
Missing, invalid, and failed leave a WriteFailure node that holds the refused handoff. handoffs_for(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, agent: str, waiting_only: bool = True) -> list[dict] What was handed to an agent, oldest first. Each has "points_to": the (label, key)
pairs to read. By default only the handoffs the agent has not accepted yet. learn(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, lesson_id: str, by: str, statement: str, supported_by, about=(), values=None, at=None) -> dict Store what was learned, with the episodes it was learned from.

  statement     the lesson, in words
  supported_by  ids of episodes that have ended. At least one.
  about         the entities it is about, as (Kind, key)
  values        other properties of the lesson

Returns a receipt {"id", "status"} with status
  learned  the lesson was stored
  exists   a lesson with this id is there already; nothing changed
  missing  an episode has not ended or does not exist, or an entity does not exist
  invalid  no statement, no episode, or something that cannot be stored
  failed   the database refused the query
Missing, invalid, and failed leave a WriteFailure node that holds the refused lesson. lesson(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, lesson_id: str) -> dict | None A lesson with its weight, the episodes for and against it, and what it is about. lessons_about(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, kind: lighthouse.kinds.Kind, key, at_least: int = 1, since=None) -> list[dict] The lessons about one entity that still hold, heaviest first. Each has "weight".

at_least  the least weight a lesson needs to be given out
since     leave out lessons that no episode has supported, contradicted, or used
          since this time: a lesson that nothing touches fades retire(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, lesson_id: str, by: str, why: str, at=None) -> dict Say that a lesson no longer holds. It stays in the graph with its evidence, and is no
longer given out. Status: retired, exists (it was retired before), or unknown. used(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, lesson_id: str, by: str, episode_id: str, helped=None, at=None) -> dict Record that a lesson was used in an episode. `helped` says whether acting on it led
to a correct result: True, False, or None while that is not known. It can be said once,
in this call or a later one. Status: used, judged, exists, or a refusal. weigh(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, lesson_id: str, by: str, episode_id: str, agrees: bool, at=None) -> dict Add an episode that ended as evidence for a lesson, or against it. An episode counts
once. Status: weighed, exists, or the refusals missing, retired, unknown. playbook(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, name: str, version: int | None = None) -> dict | None One version of a playbook with its trigger, steps, counts, and the episodes it rests
on. The newest version by default. None if there is none. playbooks_for(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, situation: dict) -> list[dict] The playbooks that are switched on and whose trigger fits a situation: every property
of the trigger is in the situation with the same value. Best record first: successes
minus failures, then runs. ran(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, name: str, by: str, episode_id: str, succeeded=None, stop_after: int = 3, at=None) -> dict Record that the newest version of a playbook ran in an episode. `succeeded` says how
it ended: True, False, or None while that is not known. It can be said once, in this
call or a later one. After `stop_after` failures in a row the playbook switches off.

Returns {"id", "status", "enabled"} with status recorded, judged, or exists; or a
refusal with status missing (the episode) or unknown (the playbook). switch(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, name: str, by: str, on: bool) -> dict Switch the newest version of a playbook on or off. Switching on clears the count of
failures in a row. Status: on, off, exists (it was so already), or unknown. write_playbook(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, name: str, by: str, trigger, steps, supported_by, needs: int = 3, at=None) -> dict Write the next version of a playbook. The version before it is switched off.

  trigger       the situation it is for: properties that must all be there
  steps         what to do, in order: a list of property maps
  supported_by  ids of the episodes it was drawn from. All must have ended.
  needs         how many episodes it must rest on (default 3)

Returns a receipt. {"id", "version", "status": "written"} when stored. Otherwise
{"id": None, "status", "reason"} with status
  missing      an episode in `supported_by` does not exist or has not ended
  unsupported  it rests on fewer episodes than it needs
  invalid      no trigger, no steps, or something that cannot be stored
  failed       the database refused the query
and a WriteFailure node that holds the refused playbook. promote(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, by: str, rule, at_least: int = 3) -> dict Read every episode that ended, ask `rule` what each one shows, and write what that
adds up to. `at_least` is how many episodes must agree before a lesson is learned or a
playbook is written (default 3).

Returns {"episodes", "lessons", "playbooks", "runs"}: how many episodes were read, and
a receipt for each lesson, playbook, and run that a claim named. Besides the statuses
of the library, a receipt can say
  waiting    fewer episodes agree than `at_least`; "for" says how many do
  unchanged  nothing new: every episode is counted, or the playbook has these steps
A lesson that is learned or weighed says how many episodes were "new" to it. between(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, kinds, relations=None, limit: int = 10, sample: int | None = None, seed: int = 1, at=None) -> list[dict] Entities by the shortest paths between other entities that run through them, highest
first: [{"entity": (label, key), "score"}]. The score is the number of such paths; where
several shortest paths join two entities, each counts for its part. Of equal scores,
the oldest entity comes first.

A path follows the direction of the relations. So an entity scores only when relations
lead into it and out of it: a relation from a kind to itself, or a chain of kinds. Where
one kind only points at another, every score is 0.
