Paths are counted from `sample` entities picked at random, and the counts are scaled up
to all: an estimate, and the same one for the same `seed`. It finds the entities that
stand out; it cannot order entities whose scores are close. The count is exact when the
sample is as large as the number of entities. Without `sample`, it is as large as WORK
allows and at least SAMPLE, so a small graph gets the exact count.

With `at`, over the relations that held at that time. The paths are counted here, not in
FalkorDB: from fewer entities for the same work, picked by `seed` in another way. connection(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, start, end, kinds=(), relations=None, max_hops: int = 6, at=None) -> list[dict] | None The shortest chain of relations from `start` to `end`, as its steps in order. None
when no chain of up to `max_hops` steps joins them, or one of them is not known. The
same thing twice is no step: [].

start, end  references: (Kind, key) for an entity, (label, id) for a record
kinds       more kinds whose relations may be followed. The kinds of start and end,
            and every kind they point at, are followed already: name a kind that
            points at both
relations   the edge types to follow, in either direction. Default: every relation of
            those kinds. Name ABOUT, CITES, and the like to go through records as well

A step is {"from", "relation", "to", "forward", "current", "since", "until"}.
  from, to  (label, key) pairs in the order of the walk. The key is None for an entity
            of a kind that was not given
  forward   False when the relation points from "to" to "from"
  current   whether the relation holds now. "since" and "until" are the start and the
            end of the last time it held; "until" is None while it holds
Where several relations join the two things of a step, the step tells of one that holds
now, and if none does, of the one that ended last.

With `at`, the shortest chain of relations that held at that time, between entities.
A step tells of a relation that held then; "current" and "until" say whether it holds
now, and when it ended. groups(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, kinds, relations=None, records=(), at_least: int = 2, limit=100, show=100, at=None) -> list[dict] Sets of things that are linked, directly or through other things, largest first:
[{"size", "members"}]. Two things are in one set when a chain of relations joins them,
whichever way the relations point.

kinds      the entities that take part: these kinds and every kind they point at
records    labels of records that take part too: Episode, Entry, Lesson, Playbook
relations  the edge types that link. Default: every relation of the kinds, and with
           records also what a record is about, has, cites, and rests on
at_least   the smallest set that is listed. 1 lists what is linked to nothing as well
"members" holds up to `show` members as (label, key) pairs, oldest first. Sets of one
size come in the order of their oldest members.

With records=["Episode"] and relations=["ABOUT"], a set holds the episodes that are
about the same entities, and those entities.

With `at`, the sets that the relations joined at that time, of the entities that existed
then. Records have no time: they cannot take part. important(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, kinds, relation=None, limit: int = 10, at=None) -> list[dict] Entities by PageRank, highest first: [{"entity": (label, key), "score"}]. Of equal
scores, the oldest entity comes first.

An entity scores high when many entities point at it, and higher when those score high
themselves. An entity shares its score evenly among what it points at; one that points
at nothing shares it among all.

The rank is taken over the entities of every kind and the edges of `relation` (default:
every relation), so the scores of all entities add up to 1. Entities of `kinds`, and of
the kinds they point at, are listed. With `at`, over the entities that existed and the
relations that held at that time. impact_of_entry(graph, entry_id: str) -> dict | None Traces every downstream record that cited or derived from `entry_id`. impact_of_state(graph, kind: lighthouse.kinds.Kind, key, since, until) -> dict Finds every record that relied on `(kind, key)` during `[since, until)`.

Returns direct entries, transitive downstream entries, derived entity states,
affected episodes, waiting handoffs, and lessons or playbooks placed at risk. invalidate_entry(graph, entry_id: str, by: str, reason: str, at=None) -> dict Marks an entry as retracted without deleting it and returns its blast radius. diff_between(graph, kinds, t1, t2) -> dict Computes the structural delta across `kinds` between `t1` and `t2`. what_if(graph, kinds, hypothetical_rows: list[tuple[lighthouse.kinds.Kind, list[dict]]], at=None, situation=None) -> dict Simulates `hypothetical_rows` in memory without writing to the database. agent_trust(graph, agent: str) -> dict How far the work of `agent` held: the counts of each kind of evidence, and "score",
from 0 to 1, or None for an agent with no evidence. The name is checked like every
name; it is not looked up as anyone's identity. context(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, user: str, session_id: str, last: int = 20) -> dict What a model needs to go on with a session: {"summary", "upto", "messages", "waiting"}.

  summary   what the messages up to number "upto" come to, or None
  messages  the messages after those, oldest first, at most `last`
  waiting   how many messages are in neither. Above 0, it is time to sum up again

A session that the user does not have gives an empty context. forget_session(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, user: str, session_id: str) -> dict Delete one session of `user`: its messages, its summary, the references that nothing
else mentions, and what was kept of its refused messages.

Returns {"id", "status", "messages"}: status "forgotten" with the number of messages
that were deleted, or "unknown" when the user has no such session.

Messages that are said while this runs are deleted with the rest. One that is said
after the session is gone opens it again. forget_user(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, user: str) -> dict Delete everything `user` said in this graph: every session, as forget_session()
does, and what was kept of every refused message. Returns {"user", "sessions",
"messages"} with how many were deleted. messages(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, user: str, session_id: str, last: int = 20, before=None) -> list[dict] The last messages of a session of `user`, oldest first, at most `last` of them. Each
has "mentions": the (label, key) pairs it names. `before` is the number of a message:
the messages just before that one are given, to read further back.

A session that the user does not have gives nothing. said(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, user: str, question: str, limit: int = 10, match: str = 'all') -> list[dict] The messages in the sessions of `user` whose text has the words of `question`, best
first. Each has "score" and "mentions".

  match  "all": every word must be there. "any": one word is enough.

Only the letters and digits of the question are used. A question without any finds
nothing. said_about(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, user: str, reference, limit: int = 20) -> list[dict] The messages in the sessions of `user` that mention one thing, newest first.
`reference` is (Kind, key) for an entity, or (label, id) for a record. say(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, user: str, session_id: str, role: str, text: str, by: str, mentions=(), values=None, at=None) -> dict Add one message to a session of `user`. The first message opens the session.

  role      who speaks, as the application names it: the user, an agent, a tool
  by        the agent or user that wrote the message
  mentions  what the message is about: entities as (Kind, key), records as (label, id)
  values    more properties of the message
  at        when it was said (default: now)

Returns a receipt. {"id", "seq", "status": "said"} when stored: the id of the session
and the number of the message in it. Otherwise {"id": None, "status", "reason"} with
  invalid  the text, the mentions, the values, or the time cannot be stored
  failed   the database refused the query
and a WriteFailure node that holds the refused message. sessions(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, user: str, limit: int = 20) -> list[dict] The sessions of `user`, the one written to last first: [{"id", "opened_at",
"active_at", "messages"}]. "messages" is how many it holds. summarize(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, user: str, session_id: str, text: str, upto: int, by: str) -> dict Store what the messages of a session up to number `upto` come to. The text is the
application's: the library holds no model. A session has one summary, and a later one
takes its place.

Returns a receipt. {"id", "upto", "status": "summed"} when stored. Otherwise
{"id": None, "status", "reason"} with status
  unknown  the user has no such session
  stale    the summary that is there reaches further than `upto`
  invalid  the text cannot be stored, or `upto` is not the number of a message
  failed   the database refused the query
and a WriteFailure node that holds the refused summary. add_task(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, task_id: str, kind: str, ref=None, after=()) -> bool Add an open task. `ref` is the key of the graph entity the task is about. `after`
lists the ids of tasks that must be done before this one can be claimed.

Returns False, and changes nothing, if a task with this id exists. Raises ValueError,
and adds nothing, if a task in `after` does not exist. claim(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, agent: str, kind: str, lease: int | None = None) -> dict | None Give the oldest free task of `kind` to `agent`: {"id", "kind", "ref", "until"}. None if
no task is free.

`lease` is how many seconds the claim holds (default: until it is done or released).
After that, another agent can claim the task, and the first can no longer complete it.
"until" is the time the lease runs out, or None. complete(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, agent: str, task_id: str) -> bool Mark a task done. Only its owner can, once; returns False otherwise. An owner whose
lease ran out can still complete the task while no other agent has claimed it. release(graph: falkordb.graph.Graph, agent: str, task_id: str) -> bool Give a claimed task back, open for another agent. Only its owner can; returns False
otherwise. now() -> str  stamp(value: str | datetime.datetime | None) -> str | None A time as `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS` in UTC, the form FalkorDB's localdatetime() parses.

FalkorDB keeps whole seconds, so fractions are dropped. A time without an offset is
taken as UTC. The client cannot send datetime parameters, so queries get this string.

title: Security and limits
text: Security and limits The memory was attacked with query text in every input, bytes the database cannot parse, values too deep or too large, oversized rows, and rows dated in the future. No input changed a query. Inputs are validated before reaching query syntax, and writes return explicit receipts. These checks do not replace application authorization or resource limits. Every attack that once did damage is now a test in lighthouse-memory/tests/test_attacks.py . What the memory does not do, and your application must - It does not know who is calling. by , the agent of a task, the receiver of a handoff, and the user of a conversation are names your code gives. Set them from an authenticated identity, in server code; never from a model's output or a person's message. - It does not decide who may read. Whoever holds a graph reads all of it. Give each tenant only its own graph. - It does not limit how often a caller writes or asks a heavy question. Each call is bounded; the number of calls is not. FalkorDB cannot stop the graph algorithms while they run, and writes wait for them. - It does not judge what a message says. Give a model what people and feeds wrote as data, never as instructions. - It erases conversations only. Do not put what a person may ask to have erased into entities, episodes, or lessons. - It does not hide refused input. Up to 2,000 characters of a refused write are kept in the graph. Integrating safely Authenticate callers before choosing a graph, user, or agent name. Expose a small set of typed functions instead of unrestricted Cypher. Validate model-proposed actions before executing them. Apply request budgets and concurrency limits outside the library, and keep database credentials and model keys on your server. See [MCP integration](/mcp), [tenant graphs](/tenants), and [model integration](/integrations). Use the [official FalkorDB security guidance](https://docs.falkordb.com/) when configuring database access. title: Memory use cases
text: Memory use cases Lighthouse Memory provides reusable building blocks for connected reasoning and persistent agent state. The patterns below describe ways to compose the library; they are not separate products shipped by the package. Security finding triage Model repositories, services, findings, and owners as Kind entities. Store each incoming observation with remember() , preserving changes and ownership history. Use pointing_at() to find findings affecting a service and connection() to explain how an exposed dependency reaches another component. Open an episode for a triage decision, append observations and proposed actions with record() , and cite the entities that support each step. A remediation worker can claim a task and receive a handoff pointing at the episode. Your integration controls whether a proposed remediation runs. Read [history](/history), [episodes](/episodes), [graph algorithms](/algorithms), and [task coordination](/coordination). Fraud investigation Represent accounts, transfers, devices, and merchants with explicit relationships. Connected components can surface groups sharing evidence; PageRank can identify structurally central entities. Neither result establishes fraud by itself. Keep investigations as episodes. Record the rule or model assessment, the supporting entities, and the human-reviewed outcome. Completed investigations can support lessons; repeated successful procedures can become playbooks under your promotion policy. When a flagged transfer turns out to be legitimate, invalidate_entry() retracts the observation without deleting it and lists the decisions, handoffs, and lessons that rested on it. Read [recall](/recall), [graph algorithms](/algorithms), [lessons and playbooks](/learning), and [audit and time travel](/audit). Codebase reasoning Represent files, symbols, dependencies, and owners as versioned entities. A dependency update becomes a new state rather than erasing the old one. Traverse connections to collect impacted components, then record the proposed change and its evidence in an episode. Your parser creates rows; your agent chooses tools; your test runner checks changes. Lighthouse stores the history, references, and coordination state between those steps. Read [the memory model](/model), [history](/history), and [MCP integration](/mcp). Agents that remember across sessions Choose a tenant graph from authenticated identity. Store messages with say() and retrieve recent context with context() . Summarize older messages using your own model, then store the result with summarize() . Use said() or said_about() to recall relevant earlier conversations. Memory persists in FalkorDB subject to the database's persistence configuration. The library does not deploy the database, authenticate a user, or choose a language model. Read [conversation memory](/conversations), [tenant isolation](/tenants), and [model integration](/integrations). A shared workflow 1. Ingest a structured observation and inspect its write receipt. 2. Retrieve connected evidence and relevant history. 3. Record the agent's decision and references in an episode. 4. Claim a task and hand context to the next worker. 5. Record the actual outcome. 6. Promote repeated evidence into lessons or playbooks using your rules. This supports both agents acting on connected data and agents sharing persistent memory. The [Python API](/reference) lists the functions behind each step.

title: Tenants
text: Tenants One FalkorDB holds many graphs, and a query never spans two. The memory uses that to keep tenants apart. python from falkordb import FalkorDB from lighthouse import tenant, world db = FalkorDB(host="127.0.0.1", port=6379) shared = world(db) the graph every tenant may read: "world" mine = tenant(db, "acme") the private graph of one tenant: "tenant:acme" - A tenant id is checked before it becomes a graph name: lowercase letters, digits, _ , and - , starting with a letter or digit, at most 63. No id can name the shared graph or another tenant's. - Give each tenant its own graph for what is theirs, such as conversations and notes, and read what everyone shares from the world graph. - A mention in a message names a thing by label and key, not by an edge, so a message in a tenant's graph can name a device in the world graph. - The memory does not decide who may read: whoever holds a graph reads all of it. Hand each tenant only its own. Application boundary Resolve the tenant and user from your authenticated identity before selecting a graph. Never let a model or request parameter choose an arbitrary graph name. The library validates names and scopes queries; connection credentials, authorization, and transport security belong to the host application. See [conversation memory](/conversations), [security limits](/security), and the [tenant API](/reference tenant).
